records.location: Levant, Mesopotamia and Arabia · regional estimate
records.finding: Arabic is widely spoken across the Levant, Mesopotamian plains and Arabia, alongside Kurdish, Armenian, Syriac, Circassian, Turkish and other languages.
Sparsely populated desert used for seasonal grazing and travel between wells.
Sparsely populated desert used for seasonal grazing and travel between wells.
Neighbouring language groups and local communities share the country between the larger regional concentrations.

Sunni Muslim communities form the largest religious group across much of Anatolia, the Levant and Arabia. Shia, Ibadi, Christian, Jewish, Druze and other communities have their own regional concentrations.
Dispersed settlements and seasonal camps occupy the country between the main towns and river valleys.
Pastoral communities move between seasonal grazing grounds and wells across the arid interior.
Cultivation is limited in the arid interior. Grazing follows rainfall, while much of the desert supports little vegetation.
Villages and small settlements spread through the countryside between the larger towns.
Cultivation and livestock rearing sustain the countryside, with trade and crafts concentrated in the towns.
Cultivated fields, pasture and uncultivated ground form a patchwork across the region.
Scattered villages and towns share the region with seasonally mobile communities.
Village farming and seasonal livestock movement sustain the northern highlands.
Cultivated valleys, pasture and uncultivated mountain land alternate across the highlands.

Ibadi Awamir pastoral communities move along the eastern edges of the Rub’ al-Khali, from the Trucial Oman hinterland towards Dhofar. Their grazing routes link the desert frontier with the settled Ibadi communities of Oman.
Shia Baharna communities predominate in the palm-growing villages and town of Qatif, alongside smaller Sunni communities.
Shia and Sunni villages share the al-Hasa oasis. Shia farming communities are established around the eastern oasis, while Hofuf and Mubarraz have predominantly Sunni populations.

Twelver Shia farming communities and centres of religious learning extend through Jabal Amil, including Nabatiya and the inland country around Tyre. Their scholars maintain close connections with Najaf.
Twelver Shia villages and notable families are established in the northern Bekaa, around Baalbek and Hermel. They share the valley with Christian and Sunni communities.
Smyrna is a major Christian centre, with a large Greek community, European residents, churches, missions and schools. The 1911 account describes the city as predominantly Christian.
Hofuf, Mubarraz and neighbouring villages form a settled oasis district.
Village farming and town markets centre on the springs and irrigated gardens.
Spring-fed canals water date plantations, gardens and fields around Hofuf and Mubarraz.
Qatif town and its palm-growing villages form a narrow settled strip beside the Gulf.
Date cultivation, fishing and coastal trade support the town and surrounding villages.
Date gardens occupy the watered coastal strip around Qatif and its villages.

genocide.title: Wartime change by January 1916
genocide.text: The Armenian genocide and deportations began in 1915. Pre-war Armenian communities and population figures cannot be read as a January 1916 resident count. In Syria and Mesopotamia, deportations also changed the population.

famine.title: Wartime change by January 1916
famine.text: Locust damage, blockade and food shortages were already affecting the Levant in 1915. These pre-war figures do not describe wartime food availability or population losses.
